title: India's Nuclear Physics History Is Not a Prelude to the Nuclear Test: Postwar State Intervention Is the Real Watershed
dek: India's early nuclear physics was in step with the West; the real watershed came with postwar state intervention. Reading it backward from the 1974 nuclear test obscures how the TIFR model damaged universities and the scientific system.
why: A concrete counter-narrative that challenges Eurocentric history of science; the middle and later sections on how big science institutions hurt universities are most valuable for policy watchers.
who: Researchers in science and technology history or science policy in emerging markets, especially research administrators concerned about national laboratory systems squeezing universities, and engineers wanting to compare China's and India's big science paths.
skip: The first 4 minutes on her academic journey can be skipped; the debate on Indian science history begins at 5:06, and the most informative part starts at 7:00.

points.h: The imperial-tool explanation does not fit Indian physics
points.body: When she entered the field, the mainstream of Indian science history was about the imperial period, with key terms like ‘imperial tools’, ‘science and empire’, ‘domestication and adaptation’, and ‘technology transfer’. She says this framework does not apply to the founders of Indian physics in the late 19th and early 20th centuries—they would not recognize themselves in these pictures. She thus wanted to push two things at once: to keep the history of post-independence Indian science from being monopolized by sociology/STS, and to question the imperial science history framework itself. Imperial institutions (geological survey, botanical survey, etc.) fit the ‘imperial tool’ explanation, but modern physics is another kind of practice.

points.h: China and India are not cases but conceptual sites
points.body: In her article with Tong Lam in History of Science, they call China and India ‘conceptual sites’ rather than ‘cases’. The origin is Armin Wong's critique of the limits of European experience: the history of science has always measured the world by European standards, so India is placed in the ‘waiting room of history’. Treating China and India as sites where the majority of the global population lives can re-establish the particularity of European experience: all knowledge is local, but claims to be universal; the ‘atypicality’ of China and India is not backwardness but an entry point for understanding how science takes root.

points.h: War, not the nuclear test, redrew the map of nuclear physics
points.body: Early nuclear physics narratives are often hijacked by hindsight from the 1974 nuclear test. She returns to the scene of 1932, when nuclear physics took shape as a discipline, and 1939, when the fission paper appeared: the two physics departments in Calcutta and Bangalore were then chasing the same frontier—Raman spoke of a particle accelerator that ‘every civilized nation should have’. War changed everything: accelerators jumped from 27 inches to hundreds of inches, the US led, and Europe's answer was CERN. After independence, India's question became: how can a new country that is not rich and lacks talent answer this resource-intensive field? Her book traces the decisions, disappointments, and small joys of three groups of researchers before and after the war, and before and after independence.

points.h: In the national laboratory contest, the old physics departments lost
points.body: The two departments tried to shape themselves as frontiers around equipment, but the scale of their ambition was not enough to match the national-level ‘national laboratory’ ambitions. The Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, conceived in Bangalore during the war and later moved to Bombay, was a new institution that ‘arose in response to the times’, and after the war it became a center that combined facilities, educational institutions, and shapers of nuclear energy and weapons programs. This explains how the accelerator as an artifact forced institutional change: when the laboratory became a ‘system’, engineering and radio skills became necessary, and the state's role was embedded in every vacuum chamber and oscillator.

points.h: Big science became the only science, draining universities
points.body: After the war, the Department of Atomic Energy became the template for organizing science in India: the later Department of Space, Department of Earth Sciences, and Department of Biotechnology were all built on it. Scientists became civil servants and state employees, and state funding dominated; the cost was that universities were stripped of trained people and resources, and only recently has India seen independent, arms-length science funding agencies. India's bureaucracy is ‘accountable for compliance, not results’, and applying that logic to science further distorts basic research. The nuclear physics laboratory model went from big science to the only science.

points.h: Even with blueprints, it won't turn; what's missing is the ecosystem
points.body: Her documentary Cyclotron is about the daily maintenance of a 1930s American machine shipped from Rochester to India in the 1960s. One detail: the US used specific sizes of screws and nuts, and for 50 years after the war, the Indian market did not have the corresponding specifications, and no manufacturer in the world still produced those parts. The team assembled it by trial and error, following circuit diagrams from books borrowed from the library. These daily routines of researchers and technicians constitute the material basis of a resource-constrained economy—even if you have the blueprints, without an ecosystem it won't turn.

points.h: The archives are full of connections; difference is a historiographical disease
points.body: She opposes writing Indian science history as a ‘history of difference’: that is a historiographical disease bred by imperial archives, ending in a very narrow racial difference theory. The connections in the archives are ready-made—C.V. Raman's idol was Helmholtz; in the 1930s, Cavendish, Göttingen, Berkeley, and Calcutta were chasing the same frontier simultaneously. But historians only apply descriptions like ‘domestication’ and ‘adaptation’ to India, which is to kick India off the list of participants. She advocates following the archives, not the historian's presupposed problem framework; the narrative of ‘incommensurable civilizations’ from 19th-century medical history is wrongly projected onto nuclear magnetic resonance, dam building, and bridge building.

points.h: The historian's job is not to make science interesting
points.body: Influenced by Bruno Latour's late essay ‘Why Has Critique Run out of Steam?’, she wants to reconfigure critique in history: from ‘deconstruction’ to ‘engagement’, asking the older philosophical question—why do we want to know. Science is shaping every everyday choice: climate, artificial intelligence, surveillance, gene technology. She thinks the historian's job is not to make science ‘interesting’ but to help practitioners and ordinary people together understand how science reshapes the horizon of choices. She says she has not yet found the path, but her next book will be driven by this reflection, not by writing methodology.
